vignette:
When Arun was detained while reporting overseas, the abuse unfolded in a room he still cannot picture in a single continuous way. What he can describe are shards: a child crying somewhere beyond a wall, a guard saying a name that now catches in his chest whenever he hears anything similar, the sudden dizziness that came with hunger, fear, and repeated blows. He remembers being forced into situations that left him convinced he had acted against his own values just to survive. Even now, when he tries to tell the story in order, the memory will not come as a coherent account. Parts are blank no matter how hard he tries to reach them, and the pieces he does have feel so extreme that he sometimes says it is like hearing about another man rather than himself.

Back in the United States, Arun returned to journalism but found the ordinary soundscape of his workday had become dangerous. In the newsroom, if a video clip in the background carried the sound of children crying, or if he became lightheaded from missing a meal, or if an interview subject had a name resembling one spoken during his detention, his body reacted before he could think. He would jerk at small noises, scan colleagues’ faces and posture for any sign of threat, and feel a rush of fear, shame, and anger that seemed out of proportion to the moment. Those same moments also pulled at the memory: not in a clear way, but as disjointed flashes and a sick sense of being dropped near something he could neither fully remember nor fully escape.

What frightened Arun almost as much as the memories was what they seemed to say about him. A crying child in a documentary clip could leave him certain that something ruined in him had become visible, that other people could look at him and see exactly what had been done and what he had done to get through it. Hearing a related name could bring back the conviction that there was something fundamentally defective about him. He had come to believe that the event had marked him in a way others would detect immediately, and that belief made every trigger feel more potent; once he started expecting exposure and judgment, he noticed the sounds, names, and bodily sensations everywhere.

Over the months, he began arranging his life around not setting any of this off. He stopped meeting former friends, especially people who had known him before the detention, because being with them made him feel too visible, too aware of the gap between who he had been and who he believed he was now. He ate less and often skipped meals, telling himself he was not hungry, though in practice restriction had become a way to manage feelings he could not otherwise control. He spent long stretches turning over how the detention might have been prevented—what article he should not have pursued, what warning signs he should have noticed, what decision had exposed him. These habits made sense to him as attempts to stay ahead of the next collapse, yet they narrowed his life and deepened his isolation.

The more isolated and underfed he became, the more easily dizziness arrived, and with it another trigger. The more he ruminated about prevention, the more he circled the same inaccessible territory in memory, straining to force a clear account and meeting instead with unreal fragments and gaps. That failure sharpened his vigilance. Because he could not hold the event together, he watched other people more closely, startled more violently at ordinary sounds, and lived with a steady readiness for harm. In those states he judged himself even more harshly: if he was still reacting like this, he thought, it must mean something was deeply wrong with him.

That sense of defectiveness fed directly into his efforts to withdraw. He avoided former social contacts not only to escape questions, but because he was convinced they would see contamination on him. At work he positioned himself near exits, kept conversations brief, and skipped shared lunches, which left him lightheaded by afternoon and more vulnerable to the bodily sensation that reminded him of detention. When he startled in the office, he saw coworkers glance over, and even neutral looks were taken as confirmation that his shame was legible. In that way the threat never stayed confined to his own body; it seemed to live in the room, in other people’s expressions, in names on email chains, in audio clips he could not control.

His attempts to master the past have not brought relief. Deliberately trying to remember has only highlighted what he cannot retrieve, and those gaps themselves have become ominous, as if the missing parts must contain proof of his moral failure. He says the unreality of the memory is one of the worst parts: if it does not feel fully real, he can never be sure it is over. Recently, after jolting at the sound of a child crying during an edit and having to leave the newsroom to steady himself, he realized how much his world had contracted. He is seeking help now because he fears he is losing both his work and any remaining closeness to other people, and because a part of him still hopes it might be possible to remember what happened without feeling that it defines what kind of man he is.
